senses.def: a priest to David
to conduct oneself, with apparent focus upon overt daily behavior
that which is difficult or impossible to understand
glosses: that which is difficult to understand
senses.comment: In 1 Corinthians 13:12 the term αἴνιγμα may be interpreted as lack of clarity in perception, so that the meaning would be ‘that which is difficult to see clearly,’ but the general usage of αἴνιγμα would seem to point to the meaning of difficulty in understanding and comprehension rather than in visual perception. For another interpretation of αἴνιγμα in 1 Corinthians 13:12, see 24.37.

senses.def: an indirect or indistinct visual image
senses.comment: For another interpretation of αἴνιγμα in 1 Corinthians 13:12, see 32.21.

senses.def: the cornerstone or capstone of a building, essential to its construction (this term occurs in the NT only figuratively in reference to Christ)
senses.comment: Some scholars have assumed that ἀκρογωνιαῖος would refer to the capstone occurring at the high point of a peaked roof, but in the NT ἀκρογωνιαῖος would probably refer to the type of stone which would have been used in the Temple in Jerusalem, and therefore it is far more likely to understand ἀκρογωνιαῖος as a cornerstone rather than a capstone of a peaked roof. It would not have referred to the keystone of an arch. Since, however, in many societies the use of ‘cornerstone’ is not known and in others it may have an entirely different function, it may be more satisfactory to use an expression such as ‘the most important stone’ or ‘the very important stone.’ This serves to describe the function and significance of the cornerstone without trying to indicate precisely its location or form.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to act contrary to the will and law of God

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: a state of sinfulness as an integral element of someone’s nature
senses.comment: The implication of this statement made in criticism of Jesus in John 9:34 was that he had not adhered rigorously to all the conventional requirements of the OT law as interpreted by the Pharisees.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: the moral consequence of having sinned
senses.comment: A number of languages make a clear distinction between the active event of committing sin and the resulting moral effect of guilt, so that one must speak of ‘committing sin’ but ‘forgiving guilt.’ This is often required in some languages since a term meaning ‘to forgive’ is literally ‘to wipe away,’ ‘to erase,’ ‘to blot out,’ or ‘to return to someone.’ The actual event of sinning often does not fit with such verb expressions, since it is not the event itself which is eliminated but the moral consequences of such an event, namely, the guilt.

senses.def: to come back to life after having once died
senses.comment: This word is also found as a variant reading: Χριστὸς καὶ ἀπέθανεν καὶ ἀνέστη καὶ ἀνέζησεν ‘Christ also died, rose, and lives again’ Romans 14:9 (apparatus).|In a number of languages there is a difficulty involved in formulating some expression for ‘resurrection’ or ‘living again,’ since such a phrase may refer to what is technically known as metempsychosis, that is to say, the rebirth of the soul in another existence, a belief which is widely held in a number of areas of south Asia. This problem may be avoided in some languages by speaking of ‘his body will live again’ or ‘his body will come back to life’ or ‘he will be the same person when he lives again.’|In Luke 15:24, ὅτι οὗτος ὁ υἱός μου νεκρὸς ἦν καὶ ἀνέζησεν ‘because this son of mine was dead and he has come back to life,’ the figurative hyperbole may reflect the practice of referring to a person as dead and then coming back to life if he has been completely separated for a time from all family relations, but then has later been discovered alive and well. It is possible, of course, that in Luke 15:24 the expression is an idiom, but it is more likely to be simply a figurative usage.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ἀναζάω[a] ‘to come back to life,’ 23.93) to begin to function, with a possible implication of the suddenness of the action
to move back to a point or area from which one has previously departed, but with more explicit emphasis upon the return (compare ὑποστρέφω[a], 15.88)
to conduct oneself, with apparent focus upon overt daily behavior
to cause something to be open (see also discussion at 79.111)
(an idiom, literally: ears open, or possibly: hearing opens) to become able to hear
senses.comment: In some languages it may be relatively meaningless to translate literally ‘his ears were opened,’ since this might mean nothing more than the removal of some wax from the ear channel. It may therefore be necessary to translate ‘his ears were made so that he could hear again’ or ‘his lack of hearing was healed.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to open a door) to make possible some opportunity
(Semitic idiom, literally: to open the mouth) to begin to speak in a somewhat formal and systematic manner
(an idiom, literally: to open the eyes) to cause someone to be able to see
glosses: to cause a blind person to see
senses.comment: A strictly literal translation of ἀνοίγω τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς ‘to open the eyes’ may be entirely misleading since it would imply simply opening the eyelids. It is accordingly much better to translate as ‘to cause to see.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to open the mouth to) to speak the complete truth to someone
glosses: to speak the whole truth to

senses.def: to lead or take away from a particular point
to lead a person away for punishment after being sentenced, frequently employed in a context of putting a condemned person to death
glosses: to lead off (to punishment or to death)
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἀπάγω in Acts 12:19, see 20.65.

senses.def: to deprive a person of life, with the implication of this being the result of condemnation by legal or quasi-legal procedures
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἀπάγω in Acts 12:19, see 56.38.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to cause someone to depart from correct behavior
to mark an extension along a route
senses.comment: Though the context of Matthew 7:13 is figurative, ἀπάγω should be interpreted in the specific sense of marking a route from one place to another.

senses.def: to accept the presence of a person with friendliness
to come to believe something to be true and to respond accordingly, with some emphasis upon the source
to recognize or acknowledge the truth of something, normally implying something good
senses.comment: See discussion of Acts 24:3 at 83.8.

senses.def: to cause someone to turn away from a previous belief
glosses: to cause to turn away from
to cause to change one’s belief
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἀποστρέφω in Acts 3:26, see 68.44. For another interpretation of ἀποστρέφω in Luke 23:14, see 88.264.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to cause someone to depart from correct behavior and thus engage in serious wrongdoing
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἀποστρέφω in Luke 23:14, see 31.70.

senses.def: to cause something to be in a place where it was formerly
to cause something to turn into or to become something else or to become removed from something or someone
(a figurative extension of meaning of ἀποστρέφω ‘to cause to turn back from,’ not occurring in the NT) to cease doing something, with the implication of rejection
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἀποστρέφω in Acts 3:26, see 31.70.

senses.def: to no longer continue to believe as one has and hence to turn away from or to reject a previous set of beliefs
to abandon a former relationship or association, or to dissociate (a type of reversal of beginning to associate)
to refuse to provide help to someone
a cryptic place name designating the territory which will be the scene of the final battle of the forces of good and evil
pertaining to experiencing happiness, implying ready and willing acceptance
pertaining to being self-caused (or possibly, without evident cause)
senses.comment: In some languages one can only express ‘opened … by itself’ in Acts 12:10 by ‘opened … nobody made it open.’

senses.def: a receptacle for carrying money or other possessions; made of leather or cloth
an alternative form of Βηθζαθά (93.430) (John 5:2, apparatus)
a very small child, even one still unborn
senses.comment: In a number of languages one must make a clear distinction between a baby after its birth and one before birth, that is, a fetus. Hence, in such languages the term employed in Luke 1:41 must be quite different from the term used in Luke 2:12.

senses.subdomain: Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
senses.def: the period of time when one is very young
glosses: childhood (probably implying a time when a child is still nursing)

senses.def: a non-immediate descendant (possibly involving a gap of several generations), either male or female
senses.comment: In Revelation 22:16 ῥίζα[b] (10.33) and γένος[a] are very similar in meaning, and it is often best to coalesce the two terms into a single expression, for example, ‘I am a descendant of David’ or ‘I belong to the lineage of David.’

senses.subdomain: Groups and Members of Groups of Persons Regarded as Related by Blood but without Special Reference to Successive Generations
senses.def: a relatively large group of persons regarded as being biologically related
senses.comment: It may be difficult in some languages to clearly distinguish between culture and race as in Mark 7:26. Sometimes this difference can be indicated by saying ‘the woman lived like a Greek, but she was a Syrophoenician’ or ‘… her parents were from Syrophoenicia.’ In translating ‘people of my own race’ in Romans 11:14, it may be necessary to say ‘all my fellow Jews’ or ‘all those people of whom I am a part’ or ‘those people who are my roots’ or ‘… my trunk,’ based on the analogy of a tree trunk and branches.

senses.def: a category or class based upon an implied derivation and/or lineage
a ring for the finger, normally made of gold or silver and usually containing the signet of the owner by which he could mark ownership and seal documents
to receive or accept an object or benefit for which the initiative rests with the giver, but the focus of attention in the transfer is upon the receiver
to accept the presence of a person with friendliness
to readily receive information and to regard it as true
to take hold of something or someone, with or without force
senses.comment: A number of languages differ radically in terms for ‘taking hold of,’ depending upon whether force is employed, whether the object is a thing or an animate being, and whether the language incorporates into a verb of ‘taking hold of’ a classification as to the objects involved, for example, long and thin, round and flat, ball-like, angular, or lumpy.

senses.subdomain: Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
senses.def: to continue in an activity or state during the night

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: unlimited duration of time, with particular focus upon the future
to lose one’s motivation to accomplish some valid goal
senses.comment: In place of a negative expression such as ‘not to give up,’ it may be better in some languages to use a positive equivalent, for example, ‘to keep on’ or ‘to continue.’

senses.def: pertaining to being willing to do something without being forced or pressured
senses.comment: In a number of languages ‘willingness’ to perform some action is expressed negatively, for example, ‘not having to’ or ‘not being forced to’ or ‘not being told one must.’ A positive expression of ‘willingness’ may be indicated idiomatically by a phrase such as ‘my heart approves.’

senses.subdomain: To Intend, To Purpose, To Plan
senses.def: pertaining to being deliberately intentional
pertaining to being free
pertaining to a person who is not a slave, either one who has never been a slave or one who was a slave formerly but is no longer
to put one’s arms around someone as an expression of affection and concern
senses.comment: It may be important in some instances to indicate the symbolic value of an embrace by some type of classifying phrase, for example, ‘to show his love for by putting his arms around’ or ‘to embrace to show affection.’

senses.def: (derivative of ἐντέλλομαι ‘to command,’ 33.329) that which is authoritatively commanded
to rule or reign by exercising authority over
to throw something on
to place something on something

senses.subdomain: Events Involving Liquids and Dry Masses
senses.def: to strike upon and into (with special reference to the action of waves)
to belong to or to come to belong to, with the possible implication of by right or by inheritance
to give careful consideration to various implications of an issue
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἐπιβάλλω in Mark 14:72, see 68.5.

senses.def: to begin an activity, with special emphasis upon the inception or possibly the suddenness with which the event takes place
senses.comment: It would also be possible to understand ἐπιβάλλω in Mark 14:72 as meaning ‘when he thought of it’ or ‘when he reflected on it’ (see 30.7).

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to lay hands on) to take a person into custody for alleged illegal activity
(a Semitic idiom, literally: one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back) to begin some activity requiring close attention but then to change one’s mind about proceeding
glosses: to start to do something and then to hesitate
to begin but have second thoughts about continuing
senses.comment: It is probably best to regard the phrase ἐπιβαλὼν τὴν χεῖρα ἐπ᾽ ἄροτρον καὶ βλέπων εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω as a part of a traditional saying referring to anyone who has second thoughts about undertaking some new or different enterprise, but the particular manner in which this is adapted to a statement concerning ‘the kingdom of God’ makes its strictly idiomatic structure somewhat doubtful.

senses.def: to stitch or sew pieces of cloth together
senses.comment: This statement in Mark 2:21 may seem entirely senseless in some societies, since it is a familiar practice to sew new cloth on an old garment; in fact, garments may be so patched that it is difficult to determine what was the original piece of cloth. It may, therefore, be important to have some type of marginal explanation.

senses.def: to engage in an activity involving considerable expenditure of effort
to be involved in business, with focus upon the work which is involved
a marker of an agent relation with numerable events, with the probable implication of comprehensiveness
to cause a state to be
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret ἐργάζομαι in Matthew 7:23 as ἐργάζομαι[c] (see 90.47).

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to do that which is good and beneficial to someone
the act of speaking to or making requests of God
senses.comment: In some languages there are a number of different terms used for prayer depending upon the nature of the content, for example, requests for material blessing, pleas for spiritual help, intercession for others, thanksgiving, and praise. There may also be important distinctions on the basis of urgency and need. The most generic expression for prayer may simply be ‘to speak to God.’ It is normally best to avoid an expression which means primarily ‘to recite.’

senses.def: a promise to God that one will do something, with the implication that failure to act accordingly will result in divine sanctions against the person in question
senses.comment: It may, however, be necessary in some languages to be somewhat more specific in rendering ‘vow,’ so that one may need to translate this expression in Acts 21:23 as ‘there are four men here who have promised God that they will do something.’

senses.subdomain: Enjoy, Take Pleasure In, Be Fond of Doing
senses.def: that which someone is fond of doing, in that it produces enjoyment
desire for physical pleasure, often sexual
sulfureous yellow, yellow as sulfur
senses.comment: Note that in Revelation 9:17 the three colors parallel three plagues, fire, smoke, and sulfur, and it may therefore be useful to translate the latter part of Revelation 9:17 as ‘they had breastplates red as fire, blue as sapphire, and yellow as sulfur.’ See also 79.37.

senses.def: a relatively small altar used for burning incense; made of wood
senses.comment: θυμιατήριον may be rendered in some languages as ‘place where incense is burned in worship of God.’ One must avoid a rendering which would imply that the altar was made of incense.

senses.def: a district to the north of Macedonia
a king of Judah mentioned in the genealogy of Jesus
the dry stalks of grain or reeds κάλαμος
senses.comment: It is difficult in 1 Corinthians 3:12 to know precisely the distinction between χόρτον ‘grass’ and καλάμην ‘straw.’ It would seem clear that καλάμην would be less valuable than χόρτον, and this might be a reference to the use of straw as a very poor thatching material. On the other hand, it could be understood as a reference to the use of straw in place of grass in the making of sun- dried bricks.

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.def: to lie down, often with the implication of some degree of incapacity

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.def: to be in a reclining position as one eats (with the focus either upon the position or the act of eating)
senses.comment: For the interpretation of ἀνάκειμαι and κατάκειμαι focusing upon eating, see 23.21.

senses.def: to eat a meal, with possible reference to the fact of the people reclining to eat
senses.comment: In biblical times there were apparently three different positions involved in the eating of a meal. People might, for example, (1) be seated on cushions around a low table or (2) be seated on chairs around a table or (3) recline on couches facing a table. Meals which involved reclining on couches would normally have been more elaborate, but the verbs ἀνάκειμαι[b] and κατάκειμαι[c] have been generalized in meaning to denote the eating of a meal without necessarily specifying the particular reclining position of those who participated in the meal.|For the translator, it may be extremely awkward to speak of ‘reclining to eat,’ since this may have connotations of people who are too lazy to sit up at the table or who are too sick to partake of an ordinary meal. It is for that reason that instead of rendering ἀνάκειμαι[b] or κατάκειμαι[c] as ‘to recline to eat,’ translators use expressions such as ‘to sit down to eat’ or ‘to eat a meal.’

senses.def: to bring something under the firm control of someone
a valley between Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives
a believer whom Jesus met on the road to Emmaus

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: (derivative of κόπριον ‘manure,’ 8.76) a pile or heap of manure
to make or create something which has not existed before
glosses: creation (in the NT, used exclusively of God’s activity in creation)

senses.def: to perform religious rites as a part of worship
(derivative of λοιδορέω ‘to slander,’ 33.393) one who engages in slandering
a state of weakness resulting from disease
a liquid measure of about nine gallons or forty liters

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: sexual intercourse of a man with a married woman other than his own spouse
senses.comment: From the standpoint of the NT, adultery was normally defined in terms of the married status of the woman involved in any such act. In other words, sexual intercourse of a married man with an unmarried woman would usually be regarded as πορνεία ‘fornication’ (88.271), but sexual intercourse of either an unmarried or a married man with someone else’s wife was regarded as adultery, both on the part of the man as well as the woman. In view of the married status of the woman being the determining factor in μοιχάω, μοιχεύω, μοιχάομαι, μοιχεία, and related terms (88.277-88.278), there is a significant contrast with πορνεύω and related expressions (88.271). πορνεύω, however, may be regarded as more generic in meaning, and thus in certain contexts including adultery.|The parallel expression to Luke 16:18 in Matthew 5:32 is somewhat different: πᾶς ὁ ἀπολύων τὴν γυναῖκα αὐτοῦ παρεκτὸς λόγου πορνείας ποιεῖ αὐτὴν μοιχευθῆναι, usually rendered as ‘anyone who divorces his wife for any cause other than fornication makes her guilty of committing adultery,’ presumably on the implication that she would marry someone else, as is implied in the final clause of Matthew 5:32.

senses.def: a young man beyond the age of puberty, but normally before marriage
senses.comment: The person referred to as a νεανίας in Acts 20:9 is called a παῖς ‘boy’ (see 9.41) in Acts 20:12. This should not be understood as identity in meaning, since the person concerned could have been of such an age that either ‘young man’ or ‘boy’ was a possible denotation. In other words, the age reference of νεανίας and παῖς overlaps in Greek. In a number of languages, however, there is a much more specific and clear-cut distinction in age grading.

senses.def: to provide instruction as to correct behavior and belief
to admonish someone for having done something wrong
senses.comment: νουθετέω in 1 Thessalonians 5:14 may also be understood in the sense of ‘to warn’ (see 33.424).

senses.def: to advise someone concerning the dangerous consequences of some happening or action
senses.comment: νουθετέω in 1 Thessalonians 5:14 may also be understood in the sense of ‘to admonish’ (see 33.418).

senses.def: a building consisting of one or more rooms and normally serving as a dwelling place (οἶκος[a] also includes certain public buildings, for example, a temple. The extension of οἶκος[a] to include temples may be the result of speaking of a temple as the dwelling place of the deity.)
senses.comment: For a discussion of certain translational problems related to οἶκος[a], see 7.3.

senses.subdomain: Groups and Members of Groups of Persons Regarded as Related by Blood but without Special Reference to Successive Generations
senses.def: the family consisting of those related by blood and marriage, as well as slaves and servants, living in the same house or homestead
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of οἶκος[b] or οἰκία[b] would be ‘those who live together’ or ‘those who have the same fence’ (this being a reference to a group of huts surrounded by a fence and thus constituting a single so-called ‘family unit’).|In Acts 7:10 οἶκος can mean the household over which Joseph was placed, or it can mean the property of Pharaoh (see 57.21).

senses.def: persons of successive generations who are related by birth
senses.comment: In biblical times the reckoning of a lineage was somewhat complex in view of certain distinctions between legal and biological relations. The focus of meaning in γένεσις[b], οἶκος[c], and πατριά[a] is not, however, the list of ancestors, but the lineage of successively related persons to which the reference person belongs. Some scholars, however, interpret γένεσις[c] history, 33.19).|In some languages a successive series of ancestors is called ‘the forefathers’ or ‘those to whom one looks back’ or ‘those who have gone ahead.’ In other languages a lineage is referred to as ‘a person’s root’ or ‘a man’s trunk’ (referring to the trunk of a tree).|In Luke 2:4 there appears to be no significant difference in meaning between οἶκος and πατριά, and in some receptor languages it would be sufficient to use a single term essentially equivalent to ‘lineage.’ The two terms appear to simply reinforce their shared meaning.

senses.def: (figurative extension of meaning of οἶκος[a] ‘house,’ 7.2) possessions associated with a house and household
senses.comment: The rendering ‘property’ seems to be far more justified by the context and by general usage than the more common meaning of ‘household’ (see 10.8).

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: (idioms, literally: house of Israel, and: house of Judah, respectively) the people of Israel as an ethnic entity
senses.comment: In translating the expression ‘the people of Israel’ it may be necessary to use an appositional phrase, for example, ‘the people, namely, Israel’ or a relative clause which also serves an appositional function, for example, ‘the people who are Israel.’ In some languages it may be preferable to use a term such as ‘nation’ followed by some expression which will indicate that Israel is simply the name of the nation, for example, ‘the nation called Israel.’

senses.def: a building consisting of one or more rooms and serving as a place of worship
a building consisting of one or more rooms and serving as a dwelling place
to be the recipient of help or favor
the capacity or ability to smell
a young person, normally below the age of puberty and without distinction as to sex
senses.comment: The term παῖς may occur with either masculine or feminine articles and corresponding adjectival attributes. These gender distinctions indicate whether the person referred to is male or female. With the masculine article or attributives one may translate παῖς[a] as ‘boy,’ and similarly with female attributives one may translate παῖς[a] as ‘girl.’

senses.def: one’s immediate offspring, but without specific reference to sex or age
senses.comment: In languages in which there is no generic term for ‘child’ or ‘offspring,’ one may use ‘son’ or ‘daughter’ or ‘son and daughter,’ singular or plural, depending upon the context.

senses.def: a slave, possibly serving as a personal servant and thus with the implication of kindly regard

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to deceive by arguments or false reasons
pertaining to being closely similar to
limit as the distant end of a space
the end point of a process, implying a conclusion of a matter
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be necessary to restructure this statement in Hebrews 6:16, for example, ‘when people are contradicting one another, an oath serves to confirm what is said and to put an end to the dispute.’

senses.def: movement of an object through the air by means of wings
senses.comment: In some languages a clear distinction is made in verbs meaning ‘to fly’ depending on whether it is a bird or an insect.

senses.def: (derivative of πλήρης[a] ‘full,’ 59.35) to cause something to become full
to make something total or complete
to finish an activity after having done everything involved
to provide for by supplying a complete amount
senses.comment: ‘To be fully provided for’ may be expressed as ‘to have all that one needs.’

senses.def: to relate fully the content of a message
to give the true or complete meaning to something
glosses: to give the true meaning to
to provide the real significance of
senses.comment: In speaking of ‘true meaning,’ it may be useful in some languages to use a phrase meaning ‘real intent’ or ‘real purpose.’

senses.def: to cause to happen, with the implication of fulfilling some purpose
(an idiom, literally: ‘to fill the heart)to cause someone to think in a particular manner, often as a means of inducing some behavior

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Duration of Time: Beginning, End
senses.def: to come to the end of a period of time, with the implication of the completion of an implied purpose or plan
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be difficult to speak of a period of time being ‘complete.’ In Luke 1:23 one may often translate as ‘when he had finished his period of service’ or even ‘when he had done his work.’ In the case of Acts 7:30, the expression ‘after forty years were completed’ may be rendered in some languages as ‘after forty years were passed’ or ‘when forty years had happened.’

senses.def: to experience a complete degree of involvement in some event or state
Porcius Festus, the successor to Felix as procurator of Palestine; see 93.376
to know about something prior to some temporal reference point, for example, to know about an event before it happens
(derivative of προγινώσκω[a] ‘to know beforehand,’ 28.6) that which is known ahead of time or before a particular temporal reference
to await with apprehension concerning impending danger or trouble
to expect something to happen, whether good or bad
to cause to exist in an evident manner
stubborn unwillingness to learn
a long seine net used in fishing
senses.comment: The σαγήνη was a long net hanging vertically in the water with floats at the upper edge and weights at the lower. It was drawn in by men working in boats or from shore. In Matthew 13:47 the actual form of the net is not so important. What is significant is that the net was sufficiently large to catch a large number of different kinds of fish.

senses.def: Sergius Paulus, the governor of Cyprus
to continue to regard closely
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand σκοπέω in Romans 16:17 as being predominantly a mental process of paying close attention in order to be prepared to respond appropriately (see 27.58).

senses.subdomain: Be Ready To Learn, Pay Attention
senses.def: (figurative extension of meaning of σκοπέω[a] ‘to notice carefully,’ 24.32) to be ready to learn about future dangers or needs, with the implication of preparedness to respond appropriately
to exert effort in continually acquiring information regarding some matter, with the implication of concern as to how to respond appropriately
to keep on giving serious consideration to something
glosses: to let one’s mind dwell on

senses.def: a silver coin worth two didrachma or approximately four denarii

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.def: to sit down with someone or to be seated with someone

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.def: to cause someone to sit down with someone
glosses: to cause to sit down with

senses.def: to undergo the same type of suffering as others do
glosses: to assume one’s share of suffering

senses.def: the movement of two or more objects to the same location
senses.comment: In a number of languages important distinctions are made in terms referring to gathering or assembling of animate beings. The distinctions are usually based upon the number of individuals, the distance which they have come, and whether or not the individuals in question constitute a membership group or whether they are merely a loose aggregation. In view of these types of distinctions, it is likely that quite different terms will be required for the various contexts listed for this set of related meanings.

senses.def: to come/go together with one or more other persons
a figurative extension of meaning of συνέρχομαι[a] ‘to come together,’ 15.123
senses.comment: In almost all languages there are euphemistic ways of speaking about sexual intercourse, and the use of γινώσκω[f] and συνέρχομαι[c] is illustrative of this in the Greek NT. It is possible to translate γινώσκω in Luke 1:34 as simply ‘for I am not married to a man,’ and likewise, συνέρχομαι in Matthew 1:18 may be rendered as ‘before they were married.’ In some languages one may use such expressions as ‘before they were joined’ or ‘before they slept together’ or ‘before they discovered one another.’

senses.def: that which is offered as a sacrifice

senses.comment: The hyssop bush may reach a height of one meter (three feet) and has a number of woody stems.|In some translations a term for ‘hyssop’ is borrowed with a classifier such as ‘plant,’ for example, ‘a branch of a plant called hyssop.’|In John 19:29 some translators have simply used ‘a twig’ or ‘a branch,’ but this may not be adequate, since some persons see a good deal of symbolism in the use of the term ‘hyssop’ because of its relationship to ritual uses in the OT.|According to an old conjecture, the text of John 19:29 could have contained the term ὑσσός ‘javelin’ (6.35) rather than ὕσσωπος ‘hyssop’ (this reading is actually found in one eleventh century minuscule manuscript), and this has been followed by the NEB translation (“they soaked a sponge with the wine, fixed it on a javelin …”), but this form of the text has very little support and is not recommended.
